sentences.text: This dinosaur featured a large frill, brow horns, a nasal horn, and unique irregular spiky bone masses on its head.
The name Coronosaurus combines Latin and Greek words for crown and lizard, referencing the crown-like appearance of extra bone plates on its skull.
The describer Michael Ryan noted that the name was inspired by the sun's corona because of the dinosaur's frill ornamentation.
Adult individuals possessed accessory epiparietal ossifications that fuse to the rear and top of the skull frill.
These unique bone masses on the frill develop from short spines that fuse together as the individual grows.
The brow horns of adults were inflated and did not project laterally over the eye sockets like those of other ceratopsians.
The animal grew to be around 5 meters long and weighed approximately 2 tonnes.
Gregory S. Paul estimated in 2010 that the body length was 5 meters and the weight was 2 tonnes.
Phillip J. Currie discovered the remains in two bone beds within the Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Philip Currie excavated these fossils between 1996 and 2000.
Studies suggest that the environment where Coronosaurus lived was an ancient coastal plain.
The Oldman Formation, where Coronosaurus fossils were found, also contains remains of various theropods, ceratopsids, hadrosaurids, and ankylosaurids.
Coronosaurus is classified as a member of the Centrosaurini subgroup of centrosaurines.

Phylogenetic analyses have yielded different results: one analysis identified Coronosaurus as the sister taxon to Styracosaurus, while a 2016 study placed it as a sister taxon to a clade formed by Centrosaurus and Spinops, separate from Styracosaurus.
The animal belongs to the parent group Centrosaurini.
Coronosaurus is classified in the family Ceratopsidae.
It is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Coronosaurus lived during the middle Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.
